bib.title: CodeScientist: End-to-End Semi-Automated Scientific Discovery with Code-based Experimentation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "CodeScientist: End-to-End Semi-Automated Scientific Discovery with Code-based Experimentation", Peter Jansen, Oyvind Tafjord, Marissa Radensky, Pao Siangliulue, Tom Hope, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder, Daniel S. Weld, Peter Clark (Allen Institute for AI, UW, Arizona, Hebrew U). The PDF shows "arXiv:2503.22708v1 [cs.AI] 20 Mar 2025" and names no conference or journal, so treat it as a preprint (ACL-style format, but no venue is printed). 2025.

COVERAGE: Pages 1-98 (all). The text extracted cleanly, 279,348 chars. Body and limitations on pp.1-10, references on p.11, and appendices A-G on pp.14-33 (rubric, meta-analysis criteria, expert comments, prompts, novelty assessments). Appendix H (pp.34-98) holds the experiment reports and generated code for 7 discoveries. I read the main text and appendices B-E and G in full. For the prompts and the H reports and code I skimmed and grepped for results, and I did not read the code line by line. Only the first 3 of the 10 appendix prompts were looked at in any depth.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- The 19 and 6 are counts of IDEAS, not experiments. CodeScientist flagged 19 of the 50 ideas where at least one of five runs gave "interesting" results, and 6 of those 19 passed both reviews. The denominator chain is about 2000 ideas generated, then 50 human-picked, then 250 runs, then 19 flagged, then 6 surviving.
  number: 19 of 50 ideas; 6 of 19 (32%)
  setup: 57 papers on agents and virtual environments, 10 codeblocks, Claude-Sonnet-3.5-1022 as the base model, human-curated ideas, 5 attempts per idea.
  quote: "CODE SCIENTIST flagged 19 of 50 ideas for human inspection where at least one of the five experiment runs produced “interesting” results" (p.6). Also: "resulting in a total of 6 discoveries (32%) that passed both external and internal review." (p.8)
  where: p.6 (Section 4.1), p.8
- "Hundreds of experiments" means exactly 250 runs: 50 ideas x 5 attempts each.
  number: 250
  quote: "Number of ideas evaluated 50 / Experiment Builder attempts per idea 5 / Total experiment attempts 250" (Table 3, p.6)
  where: p.6
- Judging used two stages. Stage 1 was 3 external reviewers. Stage 2 was one internal domain expert, who was an author.
  number: 13 of 19 (68%) passed external review; the internal reviewer then rejected 7 of those 13
  quote: "Of the 19 candidate discoveries flagged by CODE SCIENTIST, 13 (68%) were rated as meeting minimum soundness and novelty criteria by at least 2 of the 3 external reviewers. When examining the code, experiment logs, and performing replication attempts, the internal reviewer rejected 7 of these 13 discoveries" (p.8)
  where: p.8
  Reviewer details:
  - The external reviewers are "practicing research scientists in natural language processing and who have previously published in the domain". They saw only the CodeScientist-generated papers, not the code (p.6).
  - Ratings were binarized. Unsound or not-novel counted as 0. "Clearly sound", "likely sound" or "minor concerns" counted as 1 for soundness. Incremental novelty or above counted as 1 for novelty. A discovery passed external review if the majority met both thresholds.
  - The internal reviewer "essentially functioned as a 'veto'". The reviewer read the code and logs and "attempted to replicate the results with a larger number of samples".
- Of the 13 rejected discoveries, the paper gives these reasons.
  number: 6 baseline/model too simplistic; 3 effect vanished on rerun with more samples; 2 major implementation errors; 1 too little detail
  quote: "These include 6 reported discoveries where the baselines or models themselves were overly simplistic, and 3 reported discoveries where the reported effect disappeared after rerunning the experiment with a larger number of samples. 2 reported discoveries had major implementation errors discovered by the domain expert, and were rejected." (p.8)
  where: p.8
- Only 41% of the 250 experiment runs completed successfully; 59% failed.
  number: 41% / 32% / 18% / 9% / 0%
  quote: "Experiment completed successfully 41% / Debug iteration limit reached 32% / Hard experiment time limit reached 18% / Unrecoverable code generation issue 9% / Hard cost limit reached 0%" (Table 5). Also: "Currently, 59% of the experiments the planner designs are not able to be successfully implemented by the experiment builder." (p.8)
  where: p.8
- Cost and runtime per experiment.
  number: $4.23 average; 131 min; 15.8 debug iterations; 506 lines of code
  setup: N=250. Limits per experiment were 25 debug iterations, a $10 total cost, $1 LLM cost per iteration, 90 min per iteration, and 6 hours overall.
  quote: "Average debug iterations 15.8 / Average cost $4.23 / Average runtime 131 min. / Average generated code length (lines) 506". Later: "The average experiment in this work costs ≈$4, and takes approximately 2 hours to complete." (Table 3 p.6; p.10)
  where: p.6, p.10
  Total spend is not stated. It is about $1,060 if you multiply 250 by $4.23, which is my arithmetic, not the paper's.
- Models: the base model was Claude-Sonnet-3.5-1022. The planner was asked to prefer GPT-4o-mini for the experiments' own LLM calls.
  quote: "Unless otherwise stated, we use CLAUDE-SONNET-3.5-1022 as our base model for CODE SCIENTIST. We ask the planner to prefer to experiment on GPT-4O-MINI, due to its high speed and low cost." (footnote 4, p.5)
  where: p.5
  The sandbox proxy also covers Anthropic and Together.ai models.
- Human involvement is needed at 5 steps. Without it the yield drops sharply.
  number: 2 of 100 fully autonomous ideas (2%); 4 of the same 6 without expert comments
  quote: "running CODE SCIENTIST on 100 ideas generated and executed autonomously (without human input) appeared to generate 2 candidate discoveries that passed an internal review, or a 2% success rate". Also: "rerunning the benchmark of 50 ideas ... without expert human comments appears to produce 4 of the same 6 candidate discoveries" (p.9)
  where: p.9
  The paper says this is a small sample and the variance is high. The five human steps are choosing papers, writing codeblocks, selecting ideas, giving brief comments, and validating results.
- The idea funnel was filtered by a human.
  number: about 2000 ideas from 200 paper pairs, cut to 50
  quote: "approximately 2000 candidate experiment ideas ideated from 200 randomly selected combinations of papers. As a cost saving measure, a stratified sample was presented to a domain expert, until they had manually selected 50 ideas" (p.6)
  where: p.6
  Corpus: 57 papers, 10 codeblocks. Each idea got 2-3 sentences of expert comments. The authors say they cannot measure ideator recall.
- Unfaithful code is the main hazard. Example: discovery #12 reported a graph agent beating its baseline, but neither agent ever used the graph and both picked actions randomly.
  quote: "Human inspection of the code revealed that while the agent built the graph, it never used it, instead picking actions randomly." (p.8). Also: "more than half of the potential discoveries were rejected by an internal code review by a domain expert (one of the authors) for having serious issues." (p.10)
  where: p.8, p.10
  Note that the main-text count of internal vetoes (7 of 13) differs from the "more than half" wording here, which mixes in the external rejections.
- The six surviving discoveries (Table 4, p.7) are small and incremental. Human reviewers' binarized mean scores, soundness/novelty:
  - #1 State Prediction Confidence (1.0/1.0).
  - #2 Accuracy vs representational expressivity (1.0/1.0).
  - #3 Multi-stage environment generation (1.0/1.0).
  - #4 Combinatorial optimization with resistor values (1.0/1.0).
  - #5 Action prediction, only marginally above a random baseline (1.0/0.66).
  - #6 Graph-memory ReAct agent on DiscoveryWorld (0.66/0.66).
  quote: "would likely be categorized by most as normal incremental science rather than transformational discoveries" (p.10)
  where: p.7, p.10
- Idea diversity is weak even with filtering.
  quote: "most of the ideas that are generated are highly similar, or mechanical variations of one another". Embedding-cosine uniqueness filtering "still generated many duplicates". (p.8)
  where: p.8
- Weak baselines inflate results: "comparing modified REACT agents to random baselines rather than REACT baselines". Also, experiments may "evaluate on the training set" (p.9).
  where: p.9

LIMITS
- The experiments use few samples, so they have false positives and cannot detect all but the largest effects. The authors say this is fixable by spending more.
- The 6 are called "candidate discoveries" and were not independently confirmed beyond one author's review. The authors concede they may have missed unfaithful implementations.
- Validation was one internal reviewer, who was an author, plus 3 external reviewers who saw only the papers.
- The authors state there is no data on whether the system can produce transformational results.
- They cannot give a rate of discoveries per generated idea, because ideas were hand-filtered to 50.
- The ablations are too small to infer from. The authors write "impractical" for ablations with enough statistical power.
- One domain only (agents and virtual environments, mostly TextWorldExpress). Single model family.
- The models are dated: Sonnet 3.5-1022 and GPT-4o-mini.
- The code and reports were checked only for the 7 reports in Appendix H.

BUILDS ON
- Hemberg et al. 2024, genetic search and LLM as mutation operator.
- AI Scientist (Lu et al. 2024a/b), AIGS (Liu et al. 2024), Agent Laboratory (Schmidgall et al. 2025), Data-to-Paper (Ifargan et al. 2024), MLR-Copilot (Li et al. 2024), MLAgentBench (Huang et al. 2024).
- Si et al. 2024 for the uniqueness filtering.
- Radensky et al. 2024 for LLM-judge agreement.
- ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) and TextWorldExpress (Jansen and Cote 2023) are used in the codeblocks.

CODE: none worth keeping. The code in the PDF is generated experiment code, not system code. The repository is https://github.com/allenai/codescientist.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p.2: workflow of ideation, planning, build and run, reporting and meta-analysis. It marks where each human gate sits and shows the 5 independent runs per idea feeding the meta-analysis. It is the fastest way to see "semi-automated".
- Table 4, p.7: all 19 discoveries with reviewer scores and rejection reasons. This is the source for the 6 and 13 counts.
- Table 5, p.8: failure-mode breakdown.
- Table 3, p.6: cost and usage.

PROBLEMS
- Count inconsistencies in the paper:
  - The Table 4 caption says "The 11 discoveries under 'rejected'", but the table lists #7-#19, which is 13 discoveries, and the text says 13.
  - The text breakdown of reasons (6+3+2+1) sums to 12, not 13.
  - The "13 rejected" is the same set as 19 minus 6, so it is not the same 13 as "13 passed external review".
  - Footnote 6 attaches to the "6 with those discoveries provided in Table 4" wording; the footnote marker sits on a garbled sentence.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- Extraction was clean. pypdf printed only fontTools warnings. Unicode ligatures appear in the appendix H text.
- No venue is printed. The first page carries only the arXiv stamp.
- The target note's phrasing "19 candidate discoveries, of which 6 judged at least minimally sound and incrementally novel, across hundreds of automatically run experiments" is slightly loose. The 19 are flagged ideas out of 50 chosen from about 2000 (250 runs total). They were judged by 3 external reviewers plus one author who ran replication, and the system was semi-automated with 5 human steps. Consider adding those qualifiers, plus the 41% run success rate and the $4.23 per-run cost.
